newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS - TRADE GAP TOP PROBLEM FOR POLISH ECONOMY.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - TRADE GAP TOP PROBLEM FOR POLISH ECONOMY.

text.p: Poland's most difficult task this year will be to cap a quickly widening trade deficit, which could become a serious problem if current trends were not reversed, Finance Minister Marek Belka said.
"This year we could have a bigger problem with the quick growth of the (trade) deficit than on the inflation front," Belka told a Polish industry lobby group on Wednesday.

He said Poland's 1996 current account deficit, at $1.35 billion, or less than one percent of the gross domestic product (GDP), was not alarming for a developing economy but could reach serious levels if current trends were not stopped.
Belka said that presently imports were maily comprised of investment goods, needed to modernise Poland's industry which will generate economic growth in future years.
"All (Central European) country's which have been successful in transforming their economies have a current account deficit, it is a signal of growth," he said.
Belka said that in order to keep imports from growing too quickly Poland should not slow the zloty's devaluation rate and keep a lid on internal demand through tight monetary policy.
"We are in a situation where we certainly should not reduce the crawling devaluation of the zloty and we are not taking any such decisions," Belka said.

The zloty is currently devalued at a monthly rate of one percent against a basket of five western currencies which translates into an annual rate of 12.7 percent but the 1997 budget assumes a slower annual devaluation of 9.1 percent.
Belka said however that credit action was bound to grow despite a recent monetary tightening because it started from low levels after the collapse of communism eight years ago.
"The problem is that if the pace of credit growth is too fast it could yield higher inflation and faster growth of the current account deficit," Belka said.

The National Bank of Poland, which independently controls the monetary and exchange rate policy, increased obligatory reserves at the end of February to curb fast growing credit action, which boomed 44 percent in 1996.

Analysts, who warned this year's $12 billion trade gap target would be difficult to meet, said that running a trade deficit for longer periods would erode currency reserves, which were needed to pay off the country's huge foreign debt.

"In 1996 currency reserve growth slowed, this year we should see no growth....(and with low reserves) it will not be easy to meet debt payments," said Tadeusz Chroscicki, the chief analyst at the government's Centre for Strategic Studies.

Chroscicki said high reserves were needed especially in 2004-2007 when Poland was due to pay its creditors between $4 billion and $5 billion annually in line with debt reduction agreements with Poland's government and banking creditors.
Last year official currency reserves held by the central bank grew $3.1 billion to $18 billion while reserves in the whole banking system grew $1.2 billion to $21.7 billion.

Belka said that large strides would be made in bringing down inflation to the 1997 target of year-on-year 13 percent as lower customs duties, installed at the start of the year in line with international agreements, would curb price growth.
Analysts had not been as optimistic as the finance minister and expected inflation to form around year-on-year 16.3 percent in December, down from 18.1 percent in January.

"I expect larger successes with bringing down inflation to the 13 percent target level than with curbing the trade deficit...and perhaps (1997) price growth will be much lower then analysts forecast," he said.
